title: My own fruit
hook: the rational soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own fruit (Meditations 11.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: schoolmaster. Your line was lightly. Where did you carry your importance lightly? Day six hundred twenty-one.

An apple tree grows an apple, and someone else eats it. A cow makes milk, and someone else drinks it. A vine grows grapes for somebody's table. Plants and animals, Marcus says, bear fruit that others enjoy. Book eleven of the Meditations opens with Marcus noticing that there's one kind of fruit that's different, one harvest that stays with the one who grows it. Today, as book eleven begins: my own fruit.
screen: `AN APPLE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `BOOK ELEVEN OPENS.` → `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror. Marcus lists what the reasoning soul can do. It sees itself. It examines itself. It shapes itself into whatever it chooses. No plant can look at itself and decide to grow differently. We can. Second, the fruit. The fruit it bears, he says, it gathers for itself. A tree's fruit and an animal's yield are enjoyed by others. But the fruit of a well-lived life, steadiness, kindness, clear sight, belongs to the one who grew it. You don't have to wait for someone else to taste it. Third, whole at every point. Then a striking thought. A dance or a play, Marcus says, is left incomplete if it's cut off partway. But the soul reaches its own end wherever life stops. Each act done well is whole in itself, so at any moment it can say: I have what is my own. Fourth, the wide view. The soul, he goes on, ranges over the whole universe and the emptiness around it, stretches into endless time, and sees that those who come after us will see nothing new. A person of forty, he adds, with any understanding at all, has in a sense seen everything that has been and will be. He means the same patterns keep coming round. And the point holds closer to home. Look honestly at yourself, and the harvest is already yours.
screen: `IT SEES AND SHAPES ITSELF.` · `IT GATHERS ITS OWN FRUIT.` · `WHOLE WHEREVER IT STOPS.` · `THE WIDE VIEW OF TIME.` · then, large: `MY OWN FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. For a minute, look at yourself honestly, the way you'd look at a friend you love. Not judging, just seeing. What did you grow this week? Patience in one place? A kept promise? A kind word at the right time? Name one fruit. Don't wait for anyone else to notice it. Gather it yourself. Then notice one thing you'd like to shape differently, and simply set the intention. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, who said the reasoning soul sees itself, shapes itself, and gathers its own harvest, whole at every point. Today's word.
Your line: gather your own harvest. Tonight, name one good thing you grew today, and let it be enough that you know it. Day six hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations end the day with a short, honest look at themselves, naming one good thing they grew and one thing to shape differently tomorrow.

fork.reveal: a dance or play is incomplete if interrupted, he writes, but the soul completes its work wherever it stops, and can say: I have what is my own.

original.note: Greek: fruit, harvest. Marcus says the soul gathers its own karpos.

trapdoor: what you thought: be proud of yourself.
what it means: the good you grow is yours at once, and a life lived well is whole at every point.
what a scholar hears: the list of the soul's powers, seeing itself, analyzing itself, shaping itself, is a compact Stoic description of reason turned back on itself.

notes: 11.1 paraphrased: the properties of the rational soul (sees itself, analyzes itself, makes itself as it chooses, enjoys its own fruit); unlike a dance or play, it completes its purpose wherever life ends ('I have what is my own'); it traverses the universe and the void, stretches into infinite time, sees that posterity will see nothing new; the man of forty. Confirm.
Marcus was born AD 121 and most scholars date the Meditations to the 170s, so 'well past forty' is safe; confirm.

Editor review (year 2): cut the unsourced dating claim that Marcus was 'well past forty' when writing (the earlier note on this is now moot); replaced 'most living things' with 11.1's own plants-and-animals line.
